This functional definition of an AMD illustrates in effect a “system of systems” that spans the rolling stock of vehicles, the roadways on which they operate, the stations or curbfront boarding and alighting zones, and the computing and communications systems that manage operations and provide wayfinding and other services to passengers. Based on the progress of the last decade with respect to AV technology and a growing number of initial system deployments in the planning phase—as well as at least a dozen commercial AV ride-hailing service currently operating—fully functional AMDs may be realized as soon as 2030 in many locations. It is becoming equally clear that the path forward to accomplish this goal on a large scale will require new perspectives on what constitutes a district-scale “system” and the services provided within. The convergence of transportation system automation and electrification has been an area of research for more than 6 years at NLR. With respect to AMDs, this research focuses on how AVs, when deployed as light-duty BEV fleets providing on-demand mobility services, can provide the foundational transport mode from which AMDs will begin to be created and scaled. As core technologies continue to develop and mature, the timeline for AMD implementation becomes clearer. NLR’s ongoing studies in related fields continue to explore implications from 3 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. the convergence of 1) the electrification of light-duty fleets deployed with BEV propulsion systems, 2) the automation of fleets for moving people and goods, and 3) the expectation, proliferation, and adoption of on-demand passenger and goods movement. Figure 1 illustrates the envisioned components within an AMD system serving a district, which includes first-mile/last-mile (FMLM) connections to regional transit at nearby intermodal stations. Although AMDs provide local transportation, accompanying regional transit services interconnect AMDs with other communities and districts and are essential for travelers to reach other parts of the region via high-capacity and higher-speed transport services, including higher- occupancy transport modes such as traditional buses, light rail, or metro rail systems. Automated electrified transport within the AMD that is well connected to conventional regional transit is essential for meeting environmental goals, even when these long-distance transport modes still use nonautomated technologies. Within the district, the AV fleets provide circulation and FMLM services using lower-passenger- capacity vehicles with direct origin-to-destination service using telecommunications and computing technology similar to those that power modern ride-hailing services. This AMD framework includes private vehicle parking facilities at locations around the perimeter for commuters using private automobiles. The reduction—and perhaps eventual elimination—of human-controlled vehicles will increase safety for both passengers and vulnerable road users within the district.
